strengths: Addresses an important problem: learning transferable EEG representations across heterogeneous recording configurations and tasks. Combining temporal and spectral processing, electrode embeddings, and sparse experts is a plausible engineering approach.
The evaluation spans nine downstream tasks, includes both linear probing and fine-tuning, and compares against several relevant EEG foundation models.
Reports competitive results on several benchmarks, including TUEV, and provides component ablations plus experiments varying model size and pretraining data volume.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocols are critically underspecified. The paper does not document train/validation/test splits, subject separation, downstream training settings, or the number of runs underlying reported uncertainties. Pretraining uses TUEG while evaluation includes its derivative datasets TUAB, TUEV, and TUSL, without explaining exclusion of overlapping recordings or subjects. Consequently, leakage-free generalization and baseline comparability cannot be established.

The reconstruction objective has unresolved technical problems. Section 2.5 masks tokens only after cross-electrode attention in the DCM, allowing masked-channel information to enter visible representations before masking. Both reconstruction targets are learned features, but no frozen target encoder, stop-gradient scheme, or collapse-prevention mechanism is specified. Constant target representations can therefore satisfy the reconstruction losses as written.

The claimed information-lossless raw pathway is unsupported. Appendix D.1 maps each channel from T dimensions to D dimensions; the reported configuration uses 1,600 samples and embedding dimensions of 256–768. A linear projection with these dimensions cannot preserve arbitrary input signals losslessly, and reconstructing its features does not guarantee full waveform recovery.

Claims of consistent superiority across all nine tasks contradict the tables. For example, fine-tuned Uni-NTFMlarge trails CSBrain on TUSL balanced accuracy (0.7844 versus 0.8571), BIOT on ADFTD balanced accuracy (0.7661 versus 0.7763), and LaBraM on TUAB AUROC (0.8964 versus 0.9022). Several favorable differences are small relative to reported variability, without significance analysis. Linear probing is also incorrectly described as zero-shot transfer.

The central electrode-unification claim is not demonstrated. Appendix D.2 supplies sequence-index arithmetic rather than a concrete mapping across electrode standards, with no clear treatment of missing channels, padding, or montage differences. There is no held-out-montage evaluation or comparison against simpler channel embeddings or geometric positional encodings.

Novelty and causal attribution remain limited. Most components are established techniques, and the related-work section itself describes prior temporal/frequency tokenization and spatial modeling. Ablations do not control parameter count or computation, isolate the reconstruction objectives, or establish advantages over simpler fusion methods. No routing analysis supports the claimed functional specialization or neuroscience interpretability.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence is insufficient for the claimed scale. The paper provides no active-parameter counts, FLOPs, throughput, or matched-compute dense baselines. Essential architectural details, including routing k and exact encoder configurations, are missing, and the code/model links are blank in the supplied manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: learning transferable EEG representations across heterogeneous tasks and electrode configurations. Combining temporal and spectral features with spatial embeddings is a reasonable design direction.

The evaluation spans nine downstream datasets, both linear probing and fine-tuning, and several relevant foundation-model baselines. Reported results are competitive, including improved TUEV balanced accuracy and weighted F1.

Component ablations on two datasets and additional model/data scaling experiments provide useful preliminary evidence. Dataset inventories and model configuration tables document substantial experimental effort.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified to establish generalization. The manuscript does not provide reproducible subject/session-level train-validation-test splits, downstream optimization settings, or the number and meaning of repeated runs. Pretraining includes TUEG, while evaluation includes related TUH datasets; exclusion of downstream test subjects and recordings is not documented. This creates an unresolved contamination risk, rather than demonstrating leakage actually occurred.

The stated masking procedure allows information from masked electrodes to enter visible representations. Equations 5–7 perform cross-electrode attention before Section 2.5 masks the resulting tokens. Consequently, visible tokens can already contain information from electrodes selected for reconstruction. Masking before cross-electrode mixing, or an explicit leakage-prevention mechanism, is needed to substantiate the masked-prediction objective.

The reconstruction targets are inadequately justified. Equations 15–16 predict learned raw-path and frequency-path embeddings, but no frozen target encoder, stop-gradient/teacher mechanism, or other safeguard against target collapse is specified. Furthermore, the claimed 'information-lossless' raw reference maps a 1600-sample input into embeddings of dimension 256–768; the illustrated linear projection cannot preserve arbitrary inputs losslessly. Reconstructing these embeddings does not establish full waveform fidelity.

Claims of comprehensive superiority contradict the reported tables. For example, fine-tuned Uni-NTFMlarge trails BIOT on ADFTD balanced accuracy (0.7661 versus 0.7763), ContraWR on Workload (0.6644 versus 0.6755), and CSBrain on TUSL (0.7844 versus 0.8571). Its linear-probe TUAB balanced accuracy also trails both listed foundation-model baselines. Several improvements are small relative to reported variability, without statistical testing. Linear probing is also incorrectly described as zero-shot transfer.

The central electrode-unification claim is not operationally established. Appendix D.2 constructs region and intra-region indices from sequence positions, but does not specify the actual electrode-to-region mapping, consistent placement across montages, or padding and missing-channel handling. No held-out montage or controlled channel-removal experiment demonstrates the claimed unification. Learned categorical addresses and one-dimensional RoPE do not by themselves establish anatomical geometry or functional connectivity.

Novelty and efficiency are not convincingly isolated. The architecture combines established convolutional encoding, band-power features, cross-attention, positional embeddings, and sparse MoE. The related-work section itself identifies prior temporal/frequency separation and spatial modeling, but does not clearly distinguish the proposed contribution. Comparisons lack matched pretraining data and compute, and the MoE ablations lack matched-capacity or matched-compute dense controls. Active parameter counts, FLOPs, runtime, and expert-specialization analyses are absent, leaving efficiency and interpretability claims unsupported.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the configuration tables: the supplied manuscript contains no usable code link and omits important implementation details such as expert routing k, encoder specifications, and downstream pooling. Table 7 labels SEED as five-class while Table 1 evaluates it as three-class. The dual-domain loss is not ablated, so its claimed necessity is also unverified. Collectively, these methodological and evidentiary gaps place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: learning transferable EEG representations across heterogeneous recording setups and tasks. Combining temporal and spectral features, electrode embeddings, and sparse experts is a plausible architectural approach.
The reported experimental scope is substantial: approximately 28,000 hours of pretraining, nine downstream datasets, four model sizes, and both linear probing and full fine-tuning.

Results are competitive on several benchmarks. For example, the large model reports TUEV balanced accuracy of 0.6991 versus 0.6903 for CSBrain, and TDBrain balanced accuracy of 0.8369 versus 0.8281 for CBraMod.
Component ablations on two datasets and additional model/data scaling experiments provide useful initial evidence that the proposed components and pretraining scale contribute to performance.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocols are insufficiently specified. The paper does not establish subject-disjoint train/validation/test splits, windowing and overlap rules, downstream training settings, or the number of runs and meaning of the reported error bars. Because TUEG supplies most pretraining data and several downstream benchmarks derive from the same corpus, explicit subject/recording exclusion is particularly important; contamination cannot be ruled out from the manuscript.

The reconstruction objective has unresolved technical problems. Section 2.5 applies masking after cross-electrode cross-attention, allowing information from subsequently masked electrodes to enter visible tokens before masking. Moreover, reconstruction targets are learned features, without a stated frozen target encoder, stop-gradient mechanism, or other collapse prevention. The claimed 'information-lossless' raw projection is also unsupported: mapping a 1600-sample input to a lower-dimensional embedding cannot generally preserve the full signal. These issues undermine the interpretation of the objective as recovering missing EEG information.

Claims of comprehensive superiority contradict Tables 1–3. Fine-tuned Uni-NTFMlarge trails CSBrain on TUSL balanced accuracy (0.7844 versus 0.8571), BIOT on ADFTD (0.7661 versus 0.7763), and ContraWR on Workload (0.6644 versus 0.6755). Its linear-probing TUAB balanced accuracy also trails both listed foundation-model baselines. Several positive differences are small relative to reported variability, with no statistical analysis supporting the repeated claims of significant improvement. Linear probing is also incorrectly described as zero-shot transfer.

Architectural gains are not separated convincingly from additional capacity, data, and compute. The 1.9B model is compared against models such as LaBraM-Base without matched-resource experiments. MoE ablations do not establish parameter- or compute-matched dense controls, and no active parameter counts, FLOPs, throughput, or training-time comparisons substantiate efficiency claims. The dual-domain loss lacks a direct ablation.

The central electrode-unification claim is underdeveloped. Appendix D.2 supplies positional index arithmetic rather than the actual mapping from heterogeneous montages to anatomical regions and electrode slots. Handling missing electrodes, padding, bipolar derivations, and unseen montages is unclear. Learned categorical embeddings and one-dimensional RoPE do not themselves establish anatomically meaningful topology; controlled cross-montage evaluations are needed.

Novelty and neuroscience interpretations are overstated. Temporal/spectral encoders, bidirectional cross-attention, hierarchical embeddings, masked reconstruction, and sparse MoE are established components; the paper needs sharper differentiation from related EEG-specific methods, including the cited CodeBrain. There is no expert-routing analysis or physiological validation demonstrating functionally specialized experts or interpretable neural connectivity.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the configuration tables. Important details such as expert hidden dimensions, routing top-k, encoder architectures, and downstream optimization are missing. Table 7 describes SEED as a five-class dataset while the experiments use three classes. Together with the methodological and evaluation ambiguities, these omissions prevent the promising reported results from providing sufficient evidence for acceptance.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: learning transferable EEG representations across heterogeneous tasks and electrode configurations. The integration of temporal features, spectral features, hierarchical electrode embeddings, and sparse experts is a plausible engineering approach.

The evaluation covers nine downstream datasets, both linear probing and fine-tuning, and four model scales. Main results include means and standard deviations over five trials, with competitive performance particularly on TUEV and TDBrain.

The appendix provides useful additional evidence, including compute-matched dense baselines, component ablations, an STFT baseline, missing-channel tests, and a 62-to-19-channel transfer experiment. These experiments support some practical benefits of the proposed components.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocols are insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not provide reproducible train/validation/test partitions, subject/session separation, window construction, or downstream tuning procedures. TUEG dominates pretraining, while TUAB, TUEV, and TUSL are related downstream corpora; no subject- or recording-level overlap exclusion is documented. This leaves a substantial unresolved contamination risk and prevents reliable assessment of generalization or baseline comparability.

The self-supervised objective has unresolved technical problems. Section 2.5 applies masking after cross-channel dual-domain attention, so visible fused tokens can already contain information from channels subsequently masked. Equations 15–16 also reconstruct learned raw/frequency projections without specifying frozen targets, a teacher, stop-gradient, or another anti-collapse mechanism. As written, constant target encoders and matching prediction heads permit trivial reconstruction solutions. Moreover, projecting a length-1600 waveform into 256–768 dimensions cannot generally provide the claimed information-lossless reference.

The central claim of comprehensive superiority contradicts the reported tables. For example, fine-tuned Uni-NTFMlarge trails CSBrain on TUSL balanced accuracy (78.44 versus 85.71), BIOT on ADFTD balanced accuracy (76.61 versus 77.63), and ContraWR on Workload balanced accuracy (66.44 versus 67.55). Its TUAB linear-probe AUROC is below EEGPT (82.78 versus 86.62). Several favorable differences are small relative to reported variability, so claims of significant improvements require stronger statistical support.

The topology mechanism does not establish the claimed reconstruction of cortical geometry. Appendix E.2 implements learned embeddings indexed by sequence position, integer division, and modulo, without specifying an electrode-to-canonical-slot mapping that remains stable across montages. These lookups and one-dimensional RoPE do not inherently encode physical adjacency or cortical sources. The channel-removal experiments are useful but narrower than general transfer across acquisition systems, references, and previously unseen electrode layouts.

Novelty and biological interpretation are overstated. The architecture combines established convolutional encoding, band-power features, cross-attention, positional embeddings, masked reconstruction, and sparse MoE. The related-work section itself identifies prior temporal/frequency tokenization and EEG-specific spatial modeling, but does not clearly isolate the advance over these approaches. Expert-routing visualizations show usage differences, not that experts acquire biological functional specialization or prevent task interference.

Reproducibility and reporting remain incomplete despite the extensive appendix. Code links are blank, key encoder and downstream-training details are missing, and Table 7 describes SEED as five-class whereas the experiments use three classes. Table 17 labels results as the small model while reproducing the tiny-model ablation values. Although Appendix J provides valuable matched-FLOPs comparisons, it reports no uncertainty there, and theoretical FLOPs alone do not establish the claimed absence of deployment-latency increases.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: transferable EEG representations across tasks and electrode configurations. The reported pretraining corpus is substantial, and evaluation spans nine downstream datasets with both linear probing and fine-tuning.

The combination of temporal and spectral features, hierarchical electrode embeddings, and sparse experts is technically plausible. Main results include five-run variability estimates and competitive performance on several tasks, particularly TUEV.

The supplementary evaluation is extensive, including compute-matched dense baselines, component ablations, scaling experiments, channel-dropout tests, a reduced-montage experiment, and expert-routing analyses. Tables 14–15 provide useful evidence for the MoE accuracy–compute tradeoff.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocols are insufficiently specified. The paper does not establish subject/session-disjoint train, validation, and test partitions, windowing procedures, or checkpoint-selection rules. Pretraining includes TUEG while evaluation includes its related TUAB, TUEV, and TUSL corpora, without explaining exclusion of downstream test recordings or subjects. This leaves a major unresolved contamination risk rather than demonstrating clean generalization.

The reconstruction objective has unresolved technical problems. Equations 15–16 predict learned raw-path and frequency-path embeddings, but no frozen target encoder, stop-gradient/teacher mechanism, or other collapse prevention is specified. Jointly learned targets admit trivial constant solutions. Furthermore, masking occurs after cross-electrode cross-attention, allowing information from subsequently masked electrodes to enter unmasked tokens. The paper needs to clarify these choices and rule out reconstruction shortcuts.

Claims of comprehensive superiority contradict Tables 1–3. Fine-tuned Uni-NTFMlarge trails BIOT on ADFTD balanced accuracy (76.61 versus 77.63), CSBrain on TUSL (78.44 versus 85.71), and ContraWR on Workload (66.44 versus 67.55). Linear-probe TUAB balanced accuracy is below both EEGPT and NeuroLM. Several favorable differences are small relative to reported variability, without statistical evidence supporting claims of significant improvement.

The central topology claim exceeds the mechanism and evidence. Algorithm 2 constructs embeddings from flattened integer indices using division and modulo; it does not explicitly encode electrode distances, cortical geometry, or functional connectivity. The canonical mapping and handling of absent electrodes are not adequately specified. Channel-dropout and 62-to-19-channel subset experiments support robustness, but do not establish reconstruction of cortical sources or general alignment of arbitrary montages.

Novelty is insufficiently distinguished from existing work. Convolutional temporal encoders, spectral features, bidirectional cross-attention, hierarchical lookup embeddings, RoPE, and top-k MoE are established components. The paper itself identifies CodeBrain's dual temporal/frequency tokenizer but provides no direct comparison. Biological analogies and routing heatmaps do not establish the stronger claims of neural functional specialization or prevention of task interference.

The main comparisons do not isolate architectural improvements from scale and pretraining differences: the largest model has 1.9B total and 307M active parameters, while several principal competitors are much smaller. The supplementary matched-compute comparisons help, but cover only three tasks and omit variability estimates and detailed baseline training configurations. FLOPs alone also do not substantiate claims of unchanged deployment latency.

Reproducibility and reporting remain inadequate despite the lengthy appendix. Essential encoder dimensions, downstream optimization settings, montage mapping, and target-update details are missing. Table 7 labels SEED as five-class although the experiments use three classes; Table 17 labels results as Uni-NTFMsmall while reproducing the tiny-model results from Tables 1 and 4. These inconsistencies, together with the unresolved protocol and objective issues, prevent the evidence from meeting a top-tier acceptance standard.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: learning transferable EEG representations across tasks and heterogeneous electrode configurations. Combining temporal features, spectral features, spatial embeddings, and sparse experts is a plausible engineering approach.

The experimental scope is substantial: approximately 28,000 hours of pretraining, nine downstream datasets, four principal model sizes, and both linear probing and fine-tuning. Main results include means and standard deviations over five trials.

The supplementary evaluation provides useful evidence beyond the main benchmarks, including compute-matched dense baselines, an STFT baseline, component ablations, channel-dropout tests, and a 62-to-19-channel transfer experiment.
There are promising individual results. Uni-NTFMlarge achieves 69.91% balanced accuracy on TUEV, while the small MoE model consistently improves over the compute-matched dense baseline in Table 15.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocols are insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not establish downstream train/validation/test splits, subject or session separation, or checkpoint-selection procedures. Pretraining includes TUEG, while evaluation includes related TUAB, TUEV, and TUSL datasets, without explaining exclusion of overlapping evaluation recordings or subjects. This leaves a substantial unresolved contamination risk rather than establishing generalization to unseen patients.

The self-supervised objective has unresolved technical issues. Equations 15–16 reconstruct learned raw and frequency embeddings, but the paper does not specify frozen targets, a teacher, or another mechanism preventing target collapse. If these encoders are jointly optimized, constant targets and predictions admit a degenerate solution. Moreover, masking occurs after cross-electrode cross-attention, allowing information from subsequently masked electrodes to enter unmasked representations. The masking order and target-gradient treatment need clarification and validation.

Claims of comprehensive state-of-the-art performance contradict the reported tables. Fine-tuned Uni-NTFMlarge trails CSBrain on TUSL balanced accuracy (78.44% versus 85.71%) and BCIC-IV-2a (56.08% versus 56.57%), BIOT on ADFTD (76.61% versus 77.63%), and ContraWR on Workload (66.44% versus 67.55%). Linear probing also loses to EEGPT on several measures. Several positive differences are small relative to reported variability, so claims of significant superiority are not established.

The claimed reconstruction of cortical geometry is stronger than the method supports. Appendix E implements topology using categorical region, within-region, and sequence-index embeddings, without explicit geometric distances or cortical-source modeling. The canonical electrode mapping and padding rules needed to preserve identities across montages are not adequately specified. Channel-removal experiments support some robustness, but do not establish universal montage alignment or recovery of functional brain topology.

Novelty and biological interpretation are overstated. The architecture combines established convolutional encoding, band-power features, bidirectional cross-attention, positional embeddings, masked reconstruction, and Top-k MoE. The related-work section itself identifies prior temporal–frequency tokenization and EEG-specific spatial modeling, but the distinction is not convincingly isolated. Routing heatmaps show differential expert use, not demonstrated biological functional specialization or prevention of task interference.

Reproducibility and reporting remain incomplete despite extensive appendices. Downstream optimization settings, precise encoder architectures, and augmentation settings are missing. Table 7 describes SEED as five-class whereas the experiments use three classes; Table 17 labels results as the small model although they match the tiny model in Tables 1 and 4. Supplementary comparisons generally omit uncertainty. Efficiency claims rely on FLOPs rather than measured latency or memory, and the main external comparisons do not control pretraining data and model capacity.
